title: AI Giants Get 80% of Enterprise Revenue From 1% of Customers, Most of Them Living on VC
dek: OpenAI and Anthropic draw 80% of enterprise revenue from 1% of customers, and many of those are AI companies burning VC-subsidized tokens; the only ones willing to pay real money are tech itself, and when VC stops, the trillion-dollar compute bill blows up first.
why: This monologue turns the AI bubble argument from a matter of stance into a matter of structure: who each layer's customers are, where the money comes from, whose cash flow can break. Ten minutes holds a complete transmission chain, no filler.
who: AI founders, VCs and enterprise technology buyers: if you want to know how fragile the revenue of the big model vendors and cloud giants really is, this episode lays out the transmission chain clearly.

points.h: 80% of enterprise revenue rides on 1% of customers
points.body: Ramp's enterprise spending data shows that roughly 80% of OpenAI's and Anthropic's enterprise customer revenue comes from the top 1% of customers, and that ratio has not improved at all over the past three years. Ramp chief economist Ara Karazian points out that this 1% is heavily skewed toward the tech industry and AI product/service companies, a level of concentration he has not seen in any software category he tracks. The host adds the data's boundary: it does not include players like Microsoft and the big banks, but it is still representative of the overall state of AI industry spending. In other words, what actually props up the two leading model makers' enterprise revenue is not a broad mass market but a small handful of extremely free-spending customers.

points.h: The big AI spenders' money comes from VC, not revenue
points.body: This spending structure holds up largely because AI startups are kept burning by VC money. The common play is to sell subscriptions but subsidize tokens: a user on a $20-a-month subscription can burn $30, $40 or even $100 worth of tokens, with capital covering the difference. That is, the money OpenAI/Anthropic receive from these customers depends on those customers being able to keep raising. The host admits this is his intuition: the loudest voices on AI Twitter are basically VC-backed startups, and the tokens they burn internally writing code may far exceed what outside customers pay. So-called real demand, at least a large chunk of it, is really being propped up by ‘fundraising ability.’

points.h: The only ones willing to pay big for AI are tech itself
points.body: Lay out this data and the conclusion is more awkward than most people want to admit: AI has dominated every media outlet and every conference room for three straight years, nearly every company has tried it, plenty have approved big AI budgets, but the ones actually willing to spend big turn out to be, it seems, only the tech industry itself. Industries outside tech and AI barely pay high prices for large models, and there is no sign of any reversal. Worse, this small set of leading customers is itself unstable — they could easily switch to cheaper self-built open-source models, or eventually move to on-device models. The host points out that this customer structure is OpenAI's and Anthropic's real underlying exposure.

points.h: Cloud vendors have staked their fortunes on two model companies
points.body: The risk does not stop at the two labs themselves. OpenAI and Anthropic carry over $1.1 trillion in compute purchase commitments, and they are take-or-pay contracts — no matter how much is actually used or earned, the agreed amount must be paid. The compute revenue of Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle and CoreWeave is all betting that these two can pay. The figures the host cites: OpenAI contributes about 70% of Microsoft's FY26 AI revenue; UBS estimates OpenAI and Anthropic will account for 48% of Google Cloud's total revenue next year, corresponding to roughly $84 billion to $100 billion; Barclays also gives 2027 forecasts of about $40 billion for AWS and at least $50 billion for Azure. And these two companies are still losing billions of dollars a year.

points.h: The compute bill hits a reset wall in 2027
points.body: Why hasn't the bubble burst yet? Because the mortgage-style structure hasn't reached its repayment peak. These compute contracts usually start with a small prepayment, the data center capacity isn't online yet, and the real payment obligation gets heavier month by month starting next year. The host cites an analogy from a Groundbreaker article: it's like a mortgage's low teaser rate expiring — the rate was extremely low at signing, and after the reset the monthly payment balloons to unsustainable levels; at signing, every borrower assumed house prices would keep rising and they could refinance or sell, but when everyone tries to run at once, no one can get out. OpenAI's and Anthropic's massive compute commitments are the subprime of the AI bubble. The pretty big orders leave cloud vendors carrying huge revenue backlogs, while the ability to pay rests on a belief in continued growth and on VC money that keeps arriving.

points.h: NVIDIA sells cards on its customers' debt
points.body: The very top of the chain is just as dangerous. The reason hyperscalers and neoclouds buy more GPUs is demand brought by OpenAI and Anthropic; even those who build data centers to sell to third parties are only referencing the revenue backlog on the books of companies like CoreWeave and Nebius — and those companies' customers are mainly OpenAI, Anthropic or the cloud giants behind them. More glaring still, NVIDIA's customers can no longer buy GPUs out of operating cash flow alone; every purchase depends on debt remaining available. Broadcom's latest earnings also show that Anthropic and OpenAI will become its top two customers. The host closes this layer with irony: ‘Everything is normal, everything is fine, no one needs to panic.’

points.h: Bloomberg pops a new mega-deal, and no one worries
points.body: The host points out that sell-side analysts and financial media will reassure you: the smartest people and the most powerful companies don't burn money for no reason, AI demand is real, and skeptics are just cherry-picking data. But just as his own monologue is about to end, a Bloomberg terminal news alert pops up: Crusoe signs a roughly $13 billion cloud computing contract with Jane Street. The irony is that Jane Street is itself both a major CoreWeave customer and a CoreWeave shareholder — string those identities together and it is exactly a sample of the concentration risk he has described all episode. He judges it a catastrophic capital misallocation, and also the biggest collective failure of reporting in news history.

quotes.text: Per data from fintech firm Ramp, 80% of OpenAI and Anthropix Enterprise revenues come from 1% of their customers, a number that hasn't improved over the last three years.

Most businesses have been given the green light to spend a bunch of money on AI. And in the end, it seems that the only people the tech industry can get to spend money on AI is the tech industry itself.

These are, from what I can tell, take-or-pay agreements where they agree to buy that compute capacity regardless of how much capacity they actually end up using and how much revenue they actually bring in.

In other words, OpenAI and Anthropic's massive compute commitments are the subprime mortgages of the AI bubble. They signed big, beautiful deals that helped hyperscalers and neoclouds post massive revenue backlogs under the belief that nothing bad would ever happen.
Oh, and NVIDIA's customers are no longer able to buy its GPUs through cash flow alone, so all of those purchases are contingent on their constantly availability of debt.
